q: Banana and clove dominate the nose of a cloudy Bavarian wheat beer, and neither comes from the grain or the hops. What produced them?
exp: The weizen strain makes isoamyl acetate for the banana and a phenol called 4-vinyl guaiacol for the clove, and a warm ferment encourages both. Change the yeast and the style vanishes whatever the grist looks like.

q: Two versions of one Bavarian wheat beer sit on the list, one labelled hefe and the other kristall. What separates them?
opts: One is filtered, the other is not
One is markedly stronger than the other
One uses wheat and the other barley
exp: Hefe is German for yeast, so a hefeweizen keeps its sediment and is poured cloudy, often after rolling the bottle to rouse it. Kristall is the same beer filtered bright, and filtering strips much of the soft texture along with the haze.

q: Coriander seed and dried orange peel are traditional seasonings in one Belgian wheat beer, brewed with a good proportion of unmalted wheat. Which style?
exp: Unmalted wheat gives the milky haze and a soft, faintly tart palate, and the spicing survives from the centuries before hops took over. The Bavarian wheat beers use no spice at all and take their character from yeast instead.

q: German rules set a floor on how much of the grist must be wheat malt before a beer may be sold as Weissbier. Where does that floor sit?
exp: Most weissbiers in practice run between fifty and seventy percent wheat, with barley malt making up the balance for its enzymes and its husk. Wheat alone would leave the brewer with a mash that has no filter bed at all.

q: The hexagonal Authentic Trappist Product logo may be used only where a set of conditions is satisfied. Which of these is one of them?
opts: The beer exceeds six percent alcohol
The beer is brewed in the monastery
exp: Brewing on the premises under the monks' supervision, with the proceeds supporting the community and charitable work, are the tests that matter. Trappist breweries exist well outside Belgium, in the Netherlands, Italy and England among others, and the roster shifts as communities open, close or lose the label.

q: A commercial brewery licenses a monastery's name and brews the beer at its own plant some distance away. What may the result be called?
exp: Abbey is a style designation and a commercial arrangement rather than a guarantee of monastic production. The Trappist logo exists precisely to draw that line, and it is the distinction most often muddled at the table.

q: Strong, pale gold, around eight or nine percent, dry and peppery in spite of the strength, and traditionally Belgian. Which name does that beer usually carry?
exp: Pale malt with a dose of candi sugar gives strength without heaviness, and a hot vigorous ferment dries the beer right out. A dubbel is the darker, raisiny sibling sitting a step lower in strength.

q: Farms in Wallonia brewed in the cool months for their seasonal harvest workers to drink through the following summer. Which style descends from that habit?
exp: The modern style is dry, highly attenuated, peppery and refreshing rather than powerful, which is what a field worker actually needed. Farmhouse origins also mean there was never one recipe, so the family is unusually broad.

q: Hot wort is run into a wide shallow open pan under the roof and left overnight so that whatever is in the air can inoculate it. Which family of beers begins that way?
exp: The vessel is a coolship, and the resident microflora of the Senne valley outside Brussels does the work of a pitched yeast. Fermentation then continues in old oak barrels for anything from one to three years.

q: A blender marries young and old barrels, bottles the result, and the sugar still left in the young beer restarts fermentation inside the glass. Which Belgian beer is made this way?
exp: The blend gives a dry, sharply acidic, vigorously carbonated beer often compared to sparkling wine, and it is corked and caged like one. Kriek is lambic refermented on cherries, and faro is lambic sweetened with sugar.

q: Grapefruit, pine and resin, rather than earthy herbal notes, mark the hops of which pale ale tradition?
opts: American, built on Cascade and its relatives
English, built on Fuggles and Goldings
exp: Cascade was the variety that started it, and the citrus and resin signature became the calling card of American craft brewing. The English and continental varieties carry less oil and read herbal, floral and earthy instead.

q: Extra hops and a higher gravity were built into a pale ale so that it would survive months at sea on the way to a distant garrison. Which style came out of that trade?
exp: Both alcohol and hop resins resist spoilage, so the recipe was insurance as much as flavour. The modern version has kept the hops enthusiastically and quietly dropped the reason for them.

q: The word stout began in beer language as an adjective for a strong beer of any colour, and in eighteenth-century London it fixed itself permanently to one dark style. Which style was that?
exp: A brewery would list porter and stout porter side by side, and the adjective eventually walked off on its own. That history is why the two styles shade into one another rather than dividing along any clean line.

q: A dry Irish stout arrives with a dense, tight, creamy head and a soft mouthfeel that reads almost still. Which dispense gas gives it that?
exp: Nitrogen is far less soluble than carbon dioxide, so it comes out of solution as very small persistent bubbles and the beer tastes less prickly. The same beer poured on straight carbon dioxide is sharper and noticeably thinner in texture.

q: Black as ink, close to ten percent, and shipped originally from London across the Baltic to the Russian court. Which beer is that?
exp: The strength served as a preservative on a long cold sea route and as a flourish for a wealthy customer. It also cellars for years, which puts it on the short list of age-worthy beers alongside barleywine, old ale and gueuze.

q: Milk sugar goes into one dark ale for the very reason that brewer's yeast cannot ferment it. What does the beer gain?
opts: Extra bitterness, and the name dry stout
Higher alcohol, and the name imperial stout
A firmer head, and the name porter
Sweetness and body, and the name milk stout
exp: Lactose passes straight through fermentation, so it survives as residual sweetness and a fuller texture. It is also why the style is unsuitable for anyone avoiding dairy, which is worth knowing before it reaches the table.
